Hierarchy 1 description en: Date range: ~250CE - ~1200 CE. Description: " the proposed chronology suggests a long occupation of the MLR between the first millennium BC and second millennium AD".
Hierarchy 2 description en: Description: "The Early assemblage between 500 BC and AD 200 was characterized by unslipped sand-tempered roulette-impressed pottery recovered from Fati3. This variety is common to Late Stone Age/Early Iron Age sites thoughout the Sahara and Sahel. Park (2012) found this type in Tombouze phase 1 between 500-400 BC and AD 120-330. Mauny collected several examples from an unnamed site 800m east of Goundam (IFAN-SO-52-39) and Tondiarou (IFAN-MAL-55-48) presumably from basal levels. Several thick-rimmed vessels with simple roulette impressions along the inetrior lip and exterior resemble the Faïta Facies indentified in the Méma (MacDonald et al. 2003) and the Bandiagara escarpment (Bedaux & Lange 1983)."

Description: "he Middle assemblage from approximately AD 200-1000 was the most diverse and widepsread having been recovered from Fati4 Fati6 Fati7 and Fati9. Everted rim vessels with ribbing/channelling and red slip were the most numerous examples. These vessels were also burnished in small but significant numbers. Rocovered at both Gao Ancien and Tombouze these are characteristic of assemblage dating to the second half of the fisrt millenium AD (Insoll 2000; Park 2012). Other burnished wares with geometric comb impressions with a 'checkerboard' pattern of slipped and unslipped areas from the Ghourma Rharous Middle assemblage have been found around Lake Fabuibine (IFAN-MAL-55-39-4). Triangular or arced comb impressions over red burnished surfaces have been found at Djim-Djim (IFAN-MAL-55-45) El Oualadji and Killi (Lebeuf & Paques 1970: 28) and in the Gourma-Rharous (McIntosh & McIntosh 1985). These burnished comb-impressed sherds are potentially examples of the terminal Middle phase as they have been elsewhere dated to the turn of the second millennium AD (McIntosh & McIntosh 1985: 35)."

Description: "Recent assemblage ceramics were recovered in low numbers from sites Fati6 Fati8 and Fati9. Red-slipped simple open and everted rims as well as beaded rims closely resemble those of the Recent assemblage found in the Timbuktu region defined by McIntosh and McIntosh (1985). Examples include stabbing fingernail impressions and braided roulettes. Although not recovered during the survey tobacco pipes have often been associated with Recent assemblage ceramics in other regions at sites corresponding to modern villages. The limited presence of these ceramics in the Gorbi Valley may be evidence that the region was sparsely inhabited possibly in decline during the sixteenth century. For this reason this phase has been dated to AD 1000–1600."

Hierarchy 1 description en: Description: "The site of Tongo Maaré Diabal (TMD) is a habitation mound of approximately 3 to 4.5 m in elevation and 9 ha in extent. TMD was occupied from 500 CE to 1150 CE and is thus contemporary with a major expansion of urbanism in the Middle Niger as well as being situated on the periphery of the two largest known West African polities of the era: Ghana/Wagadu (c.AD 400–1100) and Kawkaw/Gao (c.AD 700–1100) "

Hierarchy 3 description en: ~800 BCE - ~10 CE. "Description: sherds trapped in granary walls two terminus post quem dates of 800 BC – 10 AD"
Description: "ritual funerary ceramics four dates on bone of 1030–1430 AD"

Hierarchy 2 description en: 13th century AD - present
7–13th century AD

Hierarchy 3 description en: The Aksumite Culture has a ceramic tradition which is widespread in central Tigray. It begins with an early phase which dates before the political unit which we know from written sources. The ceramic tradition of central Tigray (c. 1000 BC–AD 700) is represented by several sites around Yeha and Aksum (Michels 2005; Sernicola 2008). This region has been more extensively investigated and a reasonably solid cultural sequence has been outlined from the combined results of the stratigraphic sequence of the ceramics radiocarbon dating of almost fifty charcoal samples cross-dating on fragments of foreign vases and glass artefacts and coins.
Hierarchy 4 description en: Classic Aksumite phase ceramic assemblages are characterized by round basins with a ledge rim and foot-rings globular jars with high neck small bowls with foot-rings and a ledge rim often decorated with vertical corrugations alternating with bands of incised diamonds.
Hierarchy 5 Description: King of Aksumite prior to mid-6th century AD

Hierarchy 4 description en: The Early Aksumite phase (c. 50 BC–AD 150). The palaces at Aksum show a progressive increase in size from this period. In the Early Aksumite phase the shaft tombs were covered by stone platforms and were associated with carefully carved stelae. There is a continuity in material culture (particularly ceramics and funerary stelae) between the Proto-Aksumite and Early Aksumite phases at Aksum. Finally imported artefacts mainly glass vessels and beads from Aksum point to contacts with Egypt Gaul India and Nubia in the Early Aksumite phase. Early Aksumite ceramic assemblages are generally characterised with orange basins with a ledge rim and foot-rings footwashing basins square basins with architectural decorations globular jars with a high neck small bowls with foot-rings and a ledge rim and cups with a small vertical strap handle sometime decorated with vertical corrugations on the whole surface of bowls and jars.
Hierarchy 5 Description: The earliest incontrovertible and dateable mention of an Askumite King dates to about 150years later and occurs not in Askum itself but from Addi Gelamo in the eastern highlands of Tigray. GDR (Ge'ez inscription) or GDRT (inscriptions from southern Arabia) = GDR king of Askum. An estimated date of this inscription is given to c. 200 AD.Phillipson (2012) suggests that the Aksumite Kingdom may have developed by the end of the 2nd century AD.

Hierarchy 4 description en: Period between the mid-4th and the early-7th centuries AD saw Askum florescence under Christian rule. Middle Aksumite phase ceramic assemblages are characterized by cups with a ledge rim open bowls and basins sometime decorated with a cross.
Hierarchy 5 Description: King of Aksumite prior to mid-6th century AD

Hierarchy 4 description en: Byzantine and Aksumite Empires maintained close contact. Domestic pottery assemblages characterized by well-fired pink ware and decorated with Christian crosses.

The period immediately prior to the emergence of the Aksumite Kingdom. Material evidence of this period including ceramics and funerary monuments are already Aksumite in style but have distinctive traits from later Aksumite ones. This includes stone platforms associated with stelae and pit graves. In the Later Proto-Aksumite phase the monoliths become larger in size. Proto-Aksumite ceramics are characterized by very fine and hard farbrics mostly orange ware with decoration being rare.Flaked stone tool industry continues to be present along with evidence of domestic livestock including cattle sheep and goats and Near Eastern domestic crops including emmer wheat free-threshing wheat barley lentil and linseed/flax and with less certainty the Ethiopian/Eritrean domesticated crop of tef (t'ef). Included in this time phase is the presence of imported glass beads with possible origins to Ptolemaic Egypt. It was also during this time period which saw the increase of Egyptian activity on the African Red-Sea coast. The Ptolemaic dynasty of Macedonian-descended Kings who ruled Egypt from the end of the 4th century BC actively sought African war elephants mounting expeditions along the Red Sea for that purpose.Funerary evidence suggests contacts with the Kingdom of Kush (Napata/Meroe) in the Middle Nile Valley of Suday. Iron and bronze (although not in frequency) indicate links with Meroitic and Post-Meroitic Kingdoms of the late 1st Millennium BC and mid-1st Millennium AD. The origins of the Aksumite Kingdom might be traced directly back to this phase particularly at Beta Giyorgis hill. Debate exists over the end of the Proto-Aksumite period. Fattovich (2010) suggests at 40 BCE end date and Phillipson (2012) suggests at date of around 120 BCE.

Hierarchy 3 description en: Definition 1: Between the 9th and 4th centuries BC before Aksumite civilisation arose architecture inscriptions and material culture in the highlands of the Northern Horn attest religious practices of southern Arabian affinity. Non-elite settlements including at sites Mai Temenai SembelMai Chiot Ona Gudo Kidane Mahre and Giyorgis Hill to name a few are indicative of a strong continuity from earlier times. Sites include pottery flaked stone artefacts and farming economy with architecture (stone built homesteads) deriving from local inspiration. Elite settlements also occur mostly in the form of temples. These mostly served religious functions and built typically of the Sabaean Style of southern Arabia. Inscribed stonework dedicated to Almaqah (southern Arabia moon god) are also present. Stelae are also found sometimes associated with grave shafts or tombs which continue to be present until Christian times. In terms of material culture pottery was hand-made modestly decorated or undecorated. Tall flared mouth vessels (sometimes referred to as 'Torpedo-shaped' vessels or 'Form 4100 Jars' are present. Copper and copper-alloy is often found as objects mostly linked to personal adornment. As yet there is limited evidence for copper working apart from one site Hara Hot north of Asamara.Iron is absent during this period. Subsistence has been attributed mainly to pastoralism and cultivation in the form of cattle sheep and goats as well as emmer wheat barley and less confidently with tef (t'ef). There are few 'Group 1' type inscriptions otherwise referred to as 'Sabaean Inscriptions' with most inscriptions belonging to 'Group II' or 'Old Ethiopic'. Based on inscriptions it has been tentatively suggested that the earliest kingdoms developed in the Northern Horn came from Askum-Yeha region. Polities were mostly localised short-lived and non-inclusive. (Source: D.W. Phillipson. 2012. Foundation of an African Civilisation: Askum & the Northern Horn 1000 BC - AD 1300. Suffolk James Currey).Definition 2: The ceramic tradition of central Tigray (c. 1000 BC–AD 700) is represented by several sites around Yeha and Aksum (Michels 2005; Sernicola 2008). This region has been more extensively investigated and a reasonably solid cultural sequence has been outlined from the combined results of the stratigraphic sequence of the ceramics radiocarbon dating of almost fifty charcoal samples cross-dating on fragments of foreign vases and glass artefacts and coins. Two main periods of cultural development have been distinguished: the Pre-Aksumite Period (c. 1000/900–400/300 BC) and the Aksumite Period (c. 50 BC–AD 700)"
Hierarchy 4 description en: An early phase of the Pre-Aksumite Period characterized by the presence of red–orange bowls and jars red–orange bowls with a grey rim light orange ‘amphorae’ and jars and dark red jars and ‘bottles’.
Hierarchy 5 Description: Polity established linking the highland areas of Tigray and Eritrea and South Arabia. By the latter part of the first millennium BCE the South Arabian-influenced kingdom had disappeared.

Hierarchy 4 description en: The Middle Pre-Aksumite phase (c. 700/600–400 BC) is characterized by red–orange bowls and jars sometime with a grey rim dark red jars with a long neck black topped bowls and basins light orange jars and brown jars.

Definition 1: Late Pre-Aksumite Ceramics are haracterized by red–orange bowls and red-brick jars with a cylindrical neck. Definition 2: The Late Pre- Aksumite phase (c. 400/300 BC) characterized by red–orange bowls and red-brick jars with a cylindrical neck.

Hierarchy 2 description en: A broader term applied from the Eurasian Three Age System to Sudan (due to connections with Egypt along the Nile). Characterised primarily by the presence of bronze metallurgy as well as other changes variable on specific subregions. Dates given are widest possible for whole area - they vary across regions. 3700BCE - 1450BCE.
Hierarchy 3 description en: A broader term for the "Bronze Age" period within Lower Nubia generally split into the "A-Group" and "C-Group" cultural phases - the formerly defined "B-Group" phase has been since called into question. 3700BCE - 1550 BCE
Hierarchy 4 description en: The first cultural phase generally recognised for the Bronze Age of Lower Nubia. Cultivated various domestic plants and maintained domesticated sheep goats and cattle as well as hunting gathering and fishing. Some pottery styles similar to both Egypt in the North and to Upper Nubia in the South as well as a distinct "eggshell ware". Most excavation so far has focused on burials with the period particularly characterised by flexed position burials with varying grave goods. Group suddenly disappears shortly after the unification of Egypt and there is limited evidence for occupation of the area before the C-Group is visible. 3700-2800BC
Hierarchy 5 Description: A sub-period of the A-Group as based mainly on the chronology of Egyptian artefacts found within A-Group assemblages (as a result of which it is problematic and unclear). The Classic/Middle A-Group is contemporary with Naqada IId2-IIIa2. 3250BCE - 3150BCE

A sub-period of the A-Group as based mainly on the chronology of Egyptian artefacts found within A-Group assemblages (as a result of which it is problematic and unclear). The Early A-Group is contemporary with later Naqada I and Naqada IIb IIc and IIdi. 3700BCE - 3250BCE

A sub-period of the A-Group as based mainly on the chronology of Egyptian artefacts found within A-Group assemblages (as a result of which it is problematic and unclear). The Late/Terminal A-Group is contemporary with Naqada IIa2 and Dynasties 0 1 and 2. 3150BCE - 2800BCE

Hierarchy 4 description en: C-Group people were pastoralists in Lower Nubia with a distinct material culture most conspicuous through cemeteries pots and decorated bodies. They are believed to have formed an identity in contrast to contemporary Egyptians and were occupied by the Egyptians from 1937-1725BCE. They appear to have accultured to Egyptians at the end of this period. 2500BCE - 1500BCE
Hierarchy 5 Description: A sub-period of the C-Group (after Török) as based on historical association with Egyptian dynasties (the 6th-8th of the Old Kingdom and the 2nd intermediate period) and the subperiods of Kerma (part of Early Kerma). 2500BCE - 2050BCE

A sub-period of the C-Group (after Török) as based on historical association with Egyptian dynasties (the 11th-early 13th of the Middle Kingdom) and the subperiods of Kerma (Middle Kerma). 2050BCE - 1750BCE

A sub-period of the C-Group (after Török) as based on historical association with Egyptian dynasties (the developed 13th of the Middle Kingdom and the 2nd Intermediate Period) and the subperiods of Kerma (the first part of Classic Kerma). 1750BCE - 1550BCE

Hierarchy 3 description en: A broader term for the "Bronze Age" period within Upper Nubia generally defined by the Kerma culture and its precursor the Pre-Kerma. The Kerma (although possibly not the Pre-Kerma) is also defined as part of a broader Kingdom of Kush the first polity referred to as such but due to the discontinuity between this Kingdom and the later Kingdom of Kush centred around Napata and Meroe they have been defined separately here. 3500BCE - 1450 BCE.
Hierarchy 4 description en: The Pre-Kerma is a cultural period in Upper Nubia preceding the Kerma civilisation and with many similar characteristics. It also has some similarities to the A-Group of Lower Nubia especially regarding pottery.
Hierarchy 5 Description: First period of Kerman culture. Territorial authority seemingly divided but with Kerma itself as leading power. May have been the period during which the great Deffufa was built at Kerma (Bonnet 2004). Also known as Kerma Ancien.
Second period of Kerman culture. Kerma town is greatly expanded during this time reflecting its importance as a major centre. Also known as Kerma Moyen or very occasionally Old Kush II.

The development of the pottery style continues in the Recent Pre-Kerma. The pottery is similiar to the Middle Pre-Kerma. It is polished has a black top und it is rippled limited to the rim. Additionally there is a geometric incised pattern. The artefacts show similiarities to sites between the second and the fourth cataracts.

Hierarchy 4 description en: Definition 1: The kingdom of Kerma is a political entity which dominated Upper Nubia from ca. 2500 to 1500 BC. Its political centre is the city of Kerma which has extensive fortification and ritual buildings. Egypt conquers the kingdom of Kerma in the 18th dynasty after several campaigns. Around 1500 BC Kerma is destroyed and its burial ground is deserted. Definition 2: A culture based around the site of Kerma (named after a modern village in the same location) generally regarded as a precursor to the later Kingdom of Kush. It has multiple sub-periods. The central site of Kerma was eventually destroyed in the 15th century BC.
Hierarchy 5 Description: Third period of Kerman culture simultaneous with rise of First Empire of Kush. Also known as Kerma Classique.

First period of Kerman culture. Territorial authority seemingly divided but with Kerma itself as leading power. May have been the period during which the great Deffufa was built at Kerma (Bonnet 2004). Also known as Kerma Ancien.
Second period of Kerman culture. Kerma town is greatly expanded during this time reflecting its importance as a major centre. Also known as Kerma Moyen or very occasionally Old Kush II.
Late Kerma is a period of transition where the culture of Kerma disappears after Nubia was conquered by Egypt.

Hierarchy 4 description en: An independent kingdom native to Kush (Nubia) emerging after the end of the Egyptian New Kingdom occupation in the Middle Nile Region and existing as a political unit until the AD 5th century.
Hierarchy 5 Description: Period of Kushite dynasty in which the kings of Kush were buried at Napata on the Fourth Cataract. The first part of this period during the 25th Dynasty in Egypt is distinct in a variety of ways from the rest of this period and so is sometimes considered not part of the Napatan period but as it sometimes is it is included within this period.
Hierarchy 6 description en: Sudan Lower Wadi Howar Gala Abu Ahmed fortress

Hierarchy 5 Description: A transitionary period between the Meroitic kings when the later "Medieval" kingdoms of Sudan (Makuria Nobatia Alodia) were being established where there is less direct evidence for significant centralised power.
Hierarchy 6 description en: A kingdom in southern Central Sudan centering on Soba near the Nile confluence. Southernmost of the 'Nubian' kingdoms. Also known in Arabic as ‘Alwa’

A kingdom centred on Old Dongola in the Dongola Reach in Upper Nubia which became dominant over the rest of Nubia from around the 7th to 14th centuries AD. Located in the middle of the ‘Nubian’ kingdoms.
A kingdom in Lower Nubia established around the 3rd century AD. Northernmost of the 'Nubian' kingdoms. Later it was conquered by Makuria in the 7th century AD.

Hierarchy 5 Description: The Meroitic period at times also called the Meroitic Dynasty of Kingdom was born from the political consequences of the organisation of the exotic trade between Lower Nubia and Egypt after the latter acquired control over Lower Nubia between the First and Second Cataracts. The Egyptian occupation of Lower Nubia and the organisation of the trade route along the Nile contributed to the development of the settlement chain in the Nile Valley north and south of the Second Cataract. The Meroitic period starting with Arkamaniqo's reign is characterized by a proportionate development of the kingdom as a whole and not only its southern regions. Many changes and developments happened during this period notably the move of the royal burial site from the region of Napata to that of Meroe city and the development of the Meroitic hieroglyphs.

Hierarchy 2 description en: Archaeology increasingly attests the complex and cosmopolitan nature of societies in medieval Ethiopia (c. seventh to early eighteenth centuries AD). Four religious traditions are relevant to this theme: Islam Judaism. Christianity and Indigenous religions. Ethiopia's medieval archaeology is much less well known than the prehistory of the country.
Hierarchy 3 description en: Characterised by its Gondarene architecture and castles.
Jesuit missions in Medieval Ethiopia

Christianity has tended to dominate narratives of medieval Ethiopia because of its long history and links with the Solomonic Dynasty which reigned from the late thirteenth century. A further factor was its unique character: Ethiopian Christianity developed its own distinctive Indigenous traditions that attracted external attention. Christianity was extended into the countryside in the late fifth century by the arrival of monks from the Eastern Mediterranean. Lalibela is an important site.

Muslim polities developed in Ethiopia. The state of Shewa c. AD 896/897–1285 for example was centred to the north-east of modern Addis Ababa. It was absorbed by the Ifāt Sultanate which gave way in 1420 to the Sultanate of Adal. A strong regional Islamic identity developed in Ethiopia.
Hierarchy 4 description en: Harar was the capital of the sultanate of Adal the last of the three major Islamic Sultanates that existed in medieval Eastern Ethiopia.
The Sultanate of Ifat was a medieval Sunni Muslim state between the late 13th century and early 15th century. Led by the Walashma dynasty it absorbed the Sultanate of Shewa.
The Shewa sultanate was one of the oldest documented Muslim states in the Harar region.

Hierarchy 2 description en: A period in which the Middle Nile was ruled by 2-3 major kingdoms all of which had converted to Christianity by the late 6th century AD. While the term "Medieval" draws arguably problematic parallels to Europe and the Middle East and the term "Christian" is somewhat reductive and ignores the part of this period where these kingdoms were not primarily Christian the two are the only major terms used to refer to this period.
Hierarchy 3 description en: A kingdom in Lower Nubia established around the 3rd century AD. Northernmost of the 'Nubian' kingdoms. Later it was conquered by Makuria in the 7th century AD.
Group inhabiting Eastern Sudan roughly contemporary with Nobatia. Known from Egyptian texts that mention them and visible in the archaeological record.

A period in which the Middle Nile was ruled by 2-3 major kingdoms all of which had converted to Christianity by the late 6th century AD. While the term "Medieval" draws arguably problematic parallels to Europe and the Middle East and the term "Christian" is somewhat reductive and ignores the part of this period where these kingdoms were not primarily Christian the two are the only major terms used to refer to this period.

Hierarchy 4 description en: The term covers the period in Nubia and Sudan from AD 850-1100. It is subdivided into an earlier and a later phase designated Classic Christian Period I (AD 850-1000) and Classic Christian Period II (AD 1000-1100) respectively.

The term covers the period in Nubia and Sudan from AD 550-850. It is subdivided into an earlier and a later phase designated Early Christian Period I (AD 550-700) and Early Christian Period II (AD 700-850) respectively.
A small Christian kingdom based at Jebel Adda whose rulers until c.1365 were lesser kings under broader rule of the kingdom of Makuria.

The term covers the period in Nubia and Sudan from AD 1100-1400. It is subdivided into and earlier and later phase designated Late Christian Period I (AD 1100-1300) and Late Christian Period II (AD 1300-1400) respectively.
The term covers the period in Nubia and Sudan from AD 1400-1500.

Hierarchy 1 description en: This period is the era of the last great Islamic Empires. The Ottoman Empire which had started as a small Turkic state in Anatolia in the early fourteenth century emerged in the second half of the fifteenth century as a major military and political force. The Ottomans conquered Constantinople in 1453 and the Mamluk Empire in 1517. They dominated much of Anatolia the Balkans the Near East and North Africa until the dissolution of the Ottoman Empire after World War I. The Safavids who established Shia Islam as the dominant faith of Iran ruled from 1501–1722 and were the greatest dynasty to emerge from Iran. The other great dynasty that oversaw a remarkable artistic and architectural output was the Mughals. Founded by Babur the Mughals (c. 1526–1858) ruled over the largest Islamic state in the Indian subcontinent.
Hierarchy 2 description en: Parts of Northern Sudan were occupied by the Ottoman Empire from the 1560s mainly forts along the Nile
Hierarchy 3 description en: The area of the Red Sea coast particularly around the long-lasting coastal trading towns of Suakin and Masawwa was conquered over the 16th century CE by the Ottomans and administered from across the Red sea as part of the Eyalet of Habes/Habesh beginning in the mid 16th century. 1517CE - 1880CE
In 1820 Muhammad Ali conquered much of the rest of Sudan - the Ottomans had previously only conquered parts of Northern Sudan and the Red Sea coast. 1820CE - 1880CE

Hierarchy 2 description en: After the disintegration of Makuria the North of Sudan was ruled by various separate small feudal principalities which over time mostly converted from Christianity to Islam. These principalities continued to exist until the Ottoman conquest in 1820 and their rulers were often called Danaqla after the important city of Dongola. Similar events also occurred in the South although beginning slightly later after the disintegration of Alodia/Alwa and ending earlier with their coalescence under the 'Abdallab and then the Funj Sultanate. 1300CE - 1820C
Hierarchy 3 description en: The various Arab tribal federations in post-Alodia central and southern Sudan were united by 'Abdallah Jamma in the late 15th century CE before soon after being conquered by the Funj people from further south in the 16th century CE. 1475CE - 1504CE

The Islamic sultanate of Funj (also given various other names) was founded in central and southern Sudan (around their capital of Sinnar/Sennar) in the 16th century CE seemingly by a federation of people from further south along the Nile referred to as the Funj. While coexisting with the Ottoman empire for a significant amount of time the sultanate was ultimately conquered by Ottoman/Egyptian forces in 1820 after a period of decline. 1504CE - 1821CE.
Post-Medieval possibly Christian kingdom about which very little is known.

Hierarchy 2 description en: Archaeology of the post-medieval period in Ethiopia (including of the colonial period late Ethiopian Empire etc.)

After the disappearance of the medieval Nubian kingdoms the following 500 years saw new kingdoms arise across the region the most important of which were the Funj Sultanate of Sinnar and the Sultanate of Darfur. Between and around these other smaller polities were developing for example in parts of Kordofan as well as in parts of southern Sudan. Within many riverine areas even if nominally controlled by the Funj local leadership was commonly in the hands of ‘tribal’ leaders often known as meks. As elsewhere within Sudanic Africa these kingdoms often had wide horizons they and their peripheries were increasingly tied into large-scale trading networks while also sharing wide ranging cultural ties forged through the spread of Islam. Use more specific type where known.

Hierarchy 1 description en: Description: "This tradition has been recovered from every site associated by (p.39) oral tradition with the historical state of Segou. Its range of rim forms is limited (only everted thickened rims and pot lids) and its range of decoration is almost entirely different from Pre-Segovian assemblages. Likewise the paste of the Segou pottery tradition though also of tempered grog is relatively coarse with the common addition of small lateritic pebbles." Date range: 1600 CE - 1861CE.

13–19th c. AD. "These kingdoms expanded from the Niger River to the White Volta Basin. Mossi warriors exercised pressure on the Dogon of the Plain in the 15th century and controlled the territory up to today’s border of Mali and Burkina Faso causing the retreat of the Dogon to the Cliff."
A kingdom in the Kordofan region active from the 19th to early 20th century.
Colonial period where the British and the Egyptian Khedive established joint sovereignty over Sudan as outlined in the Condominium Agreement of 1899.

Hierarchy 2 description en: Italian colonisation of Ethiopia. Outposts from the period have been studied.
The period prior to 1916 when Darfur was ruled by various independent polities believing to have originated in the 12th Century CE (although this beginning is less clear). 1100CE - 1916CE
Hierarchy 3 description en: The first state in modern Darfur attested to by historical and oral sources. Believed to have been pagan. The earliest reference to a polity in the area are from 1154CE by al-Idrisi; O'Fahey estimates the "Daju hegemony" may have begun around this point in the 12th century CE. 1100CE - 1550CE

The state in Darfur which displaced the preceding Tunjur and lasted (excluding the period of Ottoman occupation) until its final conquest by the British Empire. Ruled by the Fur people (which is the origin of the term "Darfur" meaning "Land of the Fur" in Arabic) specifically the Keira dynasty. Its foundation is unclear but at the earliest happened in the early 17th century CE (O'Fahey estimates the mid-17th century CE). 1600CE - 1916CE

The second state in modern Darfur attested to by historical and oral sources which conquered or in some other way displaced the preceding Daju. May have been founded by Arabs arriving from further North or East. The earliest historical reference to the polity is in 1550 but O'Fahey believes it may have been founded somewhat earlier. It was displaced by the Keira dynasty of the Fur people in probably by the mid-17th century CE possibly earlier. 1500CE - 1650CE.

Hierarchy 2 description en: Sites dating from this period can be found all over Senegal. But the most archaeologically rich are the sites of Gorée Diouboye Fort de Sénoudébou and Tata Almamy. A number of other sites in eastern Senegal (Toumboura Fete Sylla Pouindi and Koussa) and in the historic landscapes of the Petite côte de l'atlantique (Little Atlantic Coast).
Hierarchy 3 description en: The material culture specific to this period is found almost everywhere in Senegal. Ceramics one of the most characteristic materials are generally poorly made. The pastes were coarse and the finishes sketchy. Pottery therefore tends towards stylistic and decorative simplicity. The edges are generally simple and the lips are often flattened. Decorations are rare.
This is the period of the emergence of the Fulani group.

The material culture specific to this period is found almost everywhere in Senegal. Ceramics one of the most characteristic materials are generally poorly made. The pastes were coarse and the finishes sketchy. Pottery therefore tends towards stylistic and decorative simplicity. The edges are generally simple and the lips are often flattened. Decorations are rare.

This phase is characterised by the opening up of historic sites to the products of the Atlantic trade which are associated with local ceramics. Also the sites often reveal processes of recomposition of spaces and the habitat is increasingly fortified.

The pastes were coarse and the finishes sketchy. Pottery therefore tends towards stylistic and decorative simplicity. The edges are generally simple and the lips are often flattened. Decorations are rare.

Hierarchy 1 description en: Post-colonial period of Sudan - marked by cessation of South Sudan in 2011.
Concept to be used when information pertaining to a chronological timeframe for a given site has not been provided or detailed in the original record (Alt. Not specified).
Concept to be used when term is not listed in the vocabulary.
